explanation: Real numbers (R) are the combination of two families: rational numbers (Q) and irrational numbers (Q'). A rational number can be written as p/q, where p and q are integers and q is not 0. Its decimal form either terminates (finite digits: 1/4 = 0.25, 3/8 = 0.375) or repeats a pattern forever (0.333..., 0.939393...). An irrational number cannot be written as a quotient of integers; its decimal goes on forever with no repeating pattern, like pi = 3.14159..., e = 2.71828..., or sqrt(2) = 1.41421... Every point on the number line is exactly one real number, so rational and irrational numbers fit together with no gaps: R = Q ∪ Q'.
pakistani_life_example: Shopping for cloth at the bazaar: a shopkeeper cuts 2.5 metres of fabric for a shirt (a terminating decimal — rational). The price of 1 metre is Rs 480.50 (also rational). But if you fold a 2-metre ribbon in half again and again and measure the diagonal of a square courtyard tile of side 1 m, the diagonal is sqrt(2) = 1.41421... metres — it never ends and never repeats, so it is irrational. Both kinds of numbers appear on the same measuring tape of daily life: that tape is the real number line.

worked_example.title: Locate sqrt(5) on the number line (textbook Example 2)
steps: Since sqrt(5) = 2.236..., it lies just past 2 on the number line.
Draw segment OA of length 2 units along the line, then draw AB of length 1 unit perpendicular to it at A, making a right-angled triangle OAB.
By the Pythagoras theorem: (mOB)^2 = (mOA)^2 + (mAB)^2 = 2^2 + 1^2 = 4 + 1 = 5, so mOB = sqrt(5).
With O as centre and radius mOB = sqrt(5), draw an arc that meets the number line at point P.
Then |OP| = sqrt(5), so point P represents sqrt(5) on the number line.
worked_example.answer: Point P on the number line with |OP| = sqrt(5) ≈ 2.236
worked_example.citation: PCTB Mathematics-9, page1-150.pdf PDF page 7 (printed page 5), Section 1.1.4, Example 2

practice.prompt: Follow the textbook method: locate sqrt(2) on the number line using a right-angled triangle. Which sides do you draw first?
practice.hint: sqrt(2) is close to 1. Draw OA = 1 unit on the line and AB = 1 unit perpendicular at A. Then use Pythagoras on triangle OAB.
practice.solution: Draw OA = 1 unit on the number line and AB = 1 unit perpendicular at A. In right triangle OAB: (mOB)^2 = 1^2 + 1^2 = 2, so mOB = sqrt(2). Draw an arc with centre O and radius mOB to cut the number line at P; then |OP| = sqrt(2) ≈ 1.414.
practice.citation: Method follows PCTB Mathematics-9, page1-150.pdf PDF page 7 (printed page 5), Section 1.1.4, Example 2

quiz.text: Which of these is a rational number?
quiz.explanation: 0.25 is a terminating decimal, and every terminating decimal is a rational number (0.25 = 1/4). The other three decimals go on forever without a repeating pattern, so they are irrational.
quiz.citation: PCTB Mathematics-9, page1-150.pdf PDF page 5 (printed page 3) for terminating decimals; PDF page 6 (printed page 4) for the irrational examples

quiz.text: The recurring decimal 0.333... can be written in p/q form as:
quiz.explanation: The textbook method: let x = 0.555... in Example 3 works the same way here — multiply by 10 to get 10x = 3.333..., subtract x = 0.333..., giving 9x = 3, so x = 3/9 = 1/3. The same book also lists 0.333... = 0.3-bar with 3 repeating infinitely.
quiz.citation: PCTB Mathematics-9, page1-150.pdf PDF page 6 (printed page 4) lists 0.333... as recurring; PDF page 8 (printed page 6), Example 3 shows the multiply-and-subtract method (0.5-bar = 5/9)

quiz.text: To locate sqrt(5) on the number line, the textbook draws a right-angled triangle. Which two sides does it use?
quiz.explanation: sqrt(5) = 2.236... is near 2, so the book draws mOA = 2 units along the line and mAB = 1 unit perpendicular at A. Pythagoras then gives (mOB)^2 = 2^2 + 1^2 = 5, so mOB = sqrt(5), and an arc from O marks the point P with |OP| = sqrt(5).
quiz.citation: PCTB Mathematics-9, page1-150.pdf PDF page 7 (printed page 5), Section 1.1.4, Example 2

angel_replies.text: Chalo, one more time! Real numbers R are ALL the numbers on the number line: rationals (which stop or repeat, like 0.25 or 0.333...) plus irrationals (which never stop and never repeat, like sqrt(2)). R = Q union Q'. Dekho — every point on the line is a real number.
Hint: ask yourself — does the decimal terminate (stop), repeat a pattern, or go on forever with no pattern? Stop or repeat = rational. Forever with no pattern = irrational. Try it on 0.444... first.
Ready for the test? 3 questions, only from what we just learnt — decimals, p/q form, and sqrt(5) on the number line. Take your time, beta, you can do this!

Koi baat nahi — small mistake! Re-check one thing: does the decimal STOP or REPEAT (that is rational), or does it run on FOREVER with no pattern (that is irrational)? One check, and the answer becomes clear.

marker_tasks.prompt: Walk the marker to 1/4 = 0.25 (a terminating decimal - rational).
marker_tasks.explain_correct: 0.25 stops after two digits, and every terminating decimal is a rational number (0.25 = 1/4).
marker_tasks.explain_wrong: Not there yet - 0.25 lies one quarter of the way from 0 to 1. Terminating decimals like this are rational.
marker_tasks.citation: PCTB Mathematics-9, page1-150.pdf PDF page 5 (printed page 3), Section 1.1.2

marker_tasks.prompt: Now mark sqrt(2), the famous irrational number (1.41421356237309...).
marker_tasks.explain_correct: sqrt(2) = 1.41421... goes on forever with no repeating pattern, so it is irrational.
marker_tasks.explain_wrong: sqrt(2) is just past 1 (about 1.41). Its decimal never terminates and never repeats - that is why it is irrational.
marker_tasks.citation: PCTB Mathematics-9, page1-150.pdf PDF page 6 (printed page 4), Section 1.1.3

marker_tasks.prompt: Finally, mark sqrt(5) - the number the textbook locates with the 2-1 right triangle (2.236...).
marker_tasks.explain_correct: sqrt(5) = 2.236... sits between 2 and 2.5 - exactly where the textbook's arc from O lands point P (|OP| = sqrt(5)).
marker_tasks.explain_wrong: Close! sqrt(5) = 2.236..., just past 2. The book draws OA = 2 and AB = 1, then Pythagoras gives mOB = sqrt(5).
marker_tasks.citation: PCTB Mathematics-9, page1-150.pdf PDF page 7 (printed page 5), Section 1.1.4, Example 2
